_comment: Park profiles, one entry per team id from src/data/teams.ts. This file is the deliverable interface for park identity: it holds only the decisions a human should make by hand. Derived numbers (HR / FB / GB / run factors, pitcher fatigue rate, home-field advantage) are deliberately ABSENT -- they are computed from these fields, and a hand-set one would silently disagree with the dimensions above it. Mode is FIXED: one profile per park, computed once, applied to every home game. See C:\Users\ADMIN\.opencode\plan\gpb-park-factors.md.

altitude.note: Air density. The dominant single factor. 'high' is 3,000-4,500 ft, 'extreme' is 5,000-6,500 ft. At 5,280 ft the air is about 85% as dense, so the ball carries roughly 17% farther. Breaking balls also lose bite in thin air, so altitude hurts pitching through a second channel.

altitudeFt.note: DISPLAY ONLY. This park's own height in feet, inside its band -- 'sea' is -10 to 100, 'moderate' 101 to 1,150, 'high' 3,000 to 4,500, 'extreme' 5,000 to 6,500. 'sea' is allowed below zero because below-sea-level cities are real and there is no reason to pretend otherwise; the band boundaries are NOT contiguous, so nothing in this league can be between 1,151 and 2,999 ft. THE PHYSICS STILL READS THE BAND, not this field: airDensityRatio is computed from ALTITUDE_FT[altitude], the band midpoint, exactly as before. The panel prints both numbers so the gap is visible instead of inferred. Hand-set, not derived at runtime -- a park's altitude that changed on refresh would not be a fact about the park. Generated once by tools/stampParkAltitude.ts from a hash of the team id, and now ordinary editable numbers.

seasonOffsetC.note: DISPLAY ONLY, and the strictest separation in this file. This park's own seasonal shape in Celsius from its own annual mean, April through October. The fallback is CLIMATE_MONTH_OFFSET_C[climate], so 31 of the 32 parks are unaffected by the field existing. Present on 'ars' alone, which is a Denver-shaped park: hot summer, genuinely cold spring and autumn, where the hot_dry regime's shallow curve [-2, 2, 7, 10, 11, 8, 3] would have drawn a place that barely changes across five months. NEVER read this back into airDensityRatio. The density figure uses the annual mean alone, because a park's annual mean is not the average of its seven baseball months -- the four it does not play in are systematically colder, and averaging only the played months would quietly move every park factor.

roof.note: FIXED MODE. 'retractable_closed' is deliberately NOT an option: a roof that is sometimes shut cannot be averaged into a season-long value without producing a park that does not exist. Retractable parks are entered at their open state, and a per-game override is left for the optional weather layer.

lfFt.note: Left field, wall to centre of the wall. 320-330 is a short porch; 350-362 is deep. CEILING LOWERED from 400 to 362: the corners were running away from the league, and a 398-foot corner read as a different sport from the 322-foot one. The range is the ceiling, not a description of it, so re-raising this number without re-picking the parks above it is the regression guard.

cfFt.note: Dead centre. The single most consequential distance in the park for home runs.

rfFt.note: Right field, wall to centre of the wall. The mirror of lfFt, with a slightly lower ceiling at 355. RF is the tighter of the two because the league's right-field porches are handed off to the short-corner parks, and pulling the deep end down is what leaves room for them to exist at all.

_lcfRcf.note: Left-centre and right-centre are NOT entered. They are interpolated at 12.5% of CF from each adjacent corner, because real parks are usually roughly symmetric that way. Consequence: no park can have a true short porch opposite a true monument corner. If that starts to feel wrong, widen this file to five distances.

wallHeightFt.note: 3-5 low, 6-8 standard, 10-14 tall, 20-40 monument. Converts doubles into home runs, and it is handedness-asymmetric: a short wall with a tall wall opposite gives the park two entirely different seasons.

wallColor.note: 'light' means padded white or pale brick, which absorbs more energy, so balls that would clear a dark wall become doubles and outs. A small multiplier and one of the more satisfying details to get right.

surface.note: Turf skips harder and plays up the ground-ball game and the double play, raises infield error rates, and wears on everyone who slides. Note that this engine records no batted-ball type, so a surface factor is currently a physical model and not a measurement.

grassLength.note: Deliberately separate from surface. Long grass kills bloopers and turns grounders into singles; short grass lets grounders through. Interacts with surface: they are the same outcome arriving through two doors and must not simply be added.

soilType.note: Damp clay kills hops, so grounders become singles and the double-play rate drops. Dry hard clay does the opposite. Small alone, but it compounds with surface.

climate.note: Drives ball carry and pitcher endurance through separate channels. Hot air is about 5% less dense between 15C and 30C so balls carry further, but the larger effect is fatigue: heat and humidity drain a pitching staff.

humidity.note: Kept separate from climate because the two often disagree -- one hot arid city and one hot humid city at the same temperature play very differently. Small on carry, real on fatigue.

foulGround.note: Generous foul ground means fewer balls are caught foul, which raises home run AND strikeout rates together. This is the dimension that produces the classic large-park archetype: neutral HR factor, elevated run factor.

_tierCDropped.note: The blueprint's four Tier C dimensions -- wind, batter's-box sun, sightlines/background, and drainage -- are NOT fields in this file, and their absence is a decision rather than an oversight. Each one is flavour in the blueprint's own words: sightlines has 'no defensible number exists for it', and the other three are explicitly better modelled as a per-game roll than as a fixed park constant. Adding four enums here would mean inventing coefficients for quantities the specification says have no coefficients, which is the exact risk this file exists to avoid.

flavour.note: OPTIONAL, free text, and the single home Tier C gets. It is prose for the park's character and is NEVER read by the derivation -- there is no code path from this string to an outcome weight, and there must not be one. Empty on every park right now, which `checkParks` reports rather than leaving to be noticed later. See the blueprint's Tier C: 'Only worth building if it makes the park feel like somewhere.'
